An honest comparison — including where MESH loses

Most cost-saving tools publish their best number. Independent measurement keeps finding a gap between claimed and delivered, so this page compares *methods*, and includes the rows where we lose. Competitor facts below come from each vendor's own documentation and pricing pages, checked 2026-10-22; if we have something wrong, tell us and we will correct it.

The independent findings this market needs to answer

  • Three popular open-source token trimmers (rtk, headroom, caveman), claiming 60–90%, were independently replayed over a 614M-token corpus of real coding sessions: 3.7% combined actual saving (codepointer.dev deep dive).
  • Progressive disclosure of tool schemas, modelled at ~77% token savings, measured ~13% in production, because the router it adds costs an extra round trip per novel tool call (archestra.ai bench). Per-request measurement cannot see this; per-task measurement can.
  • The best-funded commercial router ranked 12th of 12 on the independent RouterArena leaderboard while advertising 30%+ savings.
  • Our own history is on this page too: our first caching claim was 29%; our own per-task harness cut it to ~2% on busy agent traffic because the provider's cache was already doing the work. We published the correction and kept the gate that caught it. Later, our own ledger caught one of our levers *losing* money on live traffic (−$0.0063, a cache breakpoint over a volatile prefix); the loss billed against us, and the fix shipped with a test that prices both placements.

Where MESH loses, stated plainly

  • Busy interactive agents: ~29% ceiling. The provider's cache already delivers 35–40% there. Anyone promising such traffic 70% is claiming either the provider's savings or quality you will lose.
  • Already-optimised stacks: 0–5%. Our triage will tell you not to buy.
  • A free trimmer may be all you need if your waste is one obvious thing and you don't need the saving verified. MESH's value is the *verified, billable* number; if you don't need that, rtk is free.
  • Most MESH figures are simulator-measured and labelled so. The live numbers so far come from small runs (the latest: 18.2% of real spend across 30 requests, hash-chained spools committed to the repo so you can recompute it). The pilot exists to replace every number with ones from your own traffic before any fee applies.

LiteLLM, Helicone, Langfuse — what each actually does about cost

These three are excellent tools we are often mentioned alongside. They solve different problems, they are each genuinely better than MESH at those problems, and MESH reads all three of their export formats directly — if you run any of them, you are one file export away from a quote. Runbook →

LiteLLM (MIT gateway + SDK)

Better than MESH at: breadth (100+ providers behind one OpenAI-format API), production routing (six load-balancing strategies, fallbacks, cooldowns, budgets, virtual keys), community and maturity — and the core is free.

On cost specifically, as of 2026-10-22 it does have reduction levers: one-flag automatic Anthropic cache_control placement (5-minute default, 1-hour option), MCP tool-schema deferral (collapsing tool catalogues to two virtual tools), exact-match and semantic response caching, and prompt compression via a third-party sidecar (Headroom). Spend tracking prices usage against a community-maintained price map, with per-deployment overrides.

What it does not do: measure or verify the saving. There is no per-lever net accounting, no counterfactual baseline, and no customer-recomputable record. And placement without metering can lose money silently: we tested LiteLLM 1.106.4's auto-placement empirically against a system prompt carrying a per-turn timestamp — it stamped the changed block verbatim on every one of six turns, with no stability check and no signal after six consecutive zero-read responses (wire captures in our repo under evals/wire-captures/). Under Anthropic's documented billing that traffic pays the 1.25× write premium every turn and never reads — the exact loss our own ledger once caught us making, which is why MESH ships a volatility guard and nets every cache write against its reads. If you want free levers, LiteLLM ships good ones; if you need to *know what they saved, net, with the receipt* — that is the product MESH is.

Helicone (Apache-2.0 observability + AI gateway)

Better than MESH at: observability (dashboards, sessions, custom query language, alerts), a hosted multi-provider gateway with unified billing, and prompt management — a mature platform (Pro $79/mo, Team $799/mo, as of 2026-10-22).

On cost: its gateway's exact-match response caching genuinely avoids provider charges on byte-identical repeated requests — credit where due — but it does nothing for novel requests or growing agent contexts, which is where agent spend lives. It does not reduce request tokens, and for Anthropic's prompt cache the customer writes their own cache_control. Cost figures on direct integrations are self-described best-effort estimates.

Langfuse (MIT-except-ee observability)

Better than MESH at: tracing and evals depth (agent graphs, LLM-as-judge, datasets, experiments), team features, and — worth crediting plainly — cost-tracking auditability: daily automated price audits against provider sources, customer-overridable model prices, and exact-cost ingestion that can make its numbers match your invoice (Cloud from $29/mo; unlimited MIT self-host; as of 2026-10-22).

On cost reduction: none, by design — Langfuse is async observability and is never in the request path, so it cannot compact, dedupe, place cache breakpoints, or cache responses, and it does not claim to. It tells you where the money went; MESH changes what the next request costs and proves the difference.
